en: The various devas transmit the preface concerning Kāśyapa’s descent into the world. Those who had previously practiced with shared vows concealed their true form to manifest expedient means, appearing as celestial deities. Through their compassion and majesty, they subdued and welcomed beings;
they protected the people of the nation and assisted the ultimate teaching. By providing merit as a support for wisdom, they aided both the speakers and the listeners. Now, as for their enumeration:

This matter should be discussed in terms of its historical development; it is detailed in the *Tiantai Bailu* (The Hundred Records of Tiantai), which lists it according to the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" in the *Guanfo sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha’s Radiance).
Since the time Master Ciyun composed his ritual of repentance (*chánfǎ*), the arrangements for the offerings to the deities have occasionally undergone changes.

Beichan initially criticized these shifts, yet contentious debates regarding them have persisted to this day. Master Zhangnan, wishing to rectify these matters, compiled the *Tiānzhǔ zhìshì zhuàn* (Biographies of the Deities’ Manifestations); however, he still followed certain [precedents] therein.

Formerly, I also suffered from various ailments. During the Shaoxing era, I happened to reside at Jing’an Monastery in Wushu. When the venerable Lingting went to take charge of Baoge Monastery, Juyuan was also there.

We examined the "Kao Pan" [poem] by the Double Huai [Master] while in the Lotus Society; at that time, the various masters of the quarters, including Hei’an, forgot their differences through the Way and righteousness.
We frequently held refined gatherings for Chan, teaching, poetry, and prose to stimulate and uplift one another. Once, we discussed the "Heavenly Position" (Tianwei). Examining...
Ban once remarked: "At the biennial celestial assemblies, the seating arrangements often fall into disorder; it would be well for the two masters to debate and rectify them so that no errors remain.
Later, after they had retired from public life, they dispersed in different directions—north and south—for more than fifteen years.

We have merely debated these matters from time to time amidst draft manuscripts, occasionally encountering them upon old scrolls. Yet, when reflecting back on those former assemblies, they truly seem like faded dust.
Having emerged from the state of emptiness, he came to visit Jing’an, where he found that the *Revised Compilation of the Biographies of Celestial Beings* (*Tianzhuan*) had already been completed.

Upon examining it in detail, he realized it was far more than a mere revision or embellishment of the old biographies. Furthermore, it included supplementary entries from the sutras, śāstras, and celestial phenomena;

it rectified previous errors, established two distinct categories, clarified the sequence of the arrangements, and provided individual eulogies for each—truly a work worthy of being called a beginning.

The ultimate completeness has now been achieved. Thus, while this literature was first drafted at Zhangnan, it reached its final perfection at Jing’an. It causes the stagnations of past and present to dissolve like ice melting away;
truly, it serves as a great aid to its dissemination. Furthermore, I rejoice that I have not failed the charge entrusted to me by Kaopan.
I have therefore urged for its publication to widely benefit all who see and hear it, and I venture to write these words at the head of the volume to inform those yet to come.
Recorded ten days before the arrival of the First Yang in the Gui-si year of the Qian Dao era. Transmitted by the expounder of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations, Shi Fenggui.
Preface to the Re-edited Biographies of the Various Heavens (with preface), composed by Shi Xingting of Wu-shu.
Formerly, Master Huàn of Zhāngnán remarked that the arrangement of celestial positions lacked the proper order of honor and subordination and was devoid of the ritual protocols of *zhāomù*.
Lamenting that this custom had persisted for so long without anyone correcting it, he examined the *Tripitaka* and composed the *Biographies of the Various Heavens*.
While his pioneering achievement is truly commendable, as for the sequence of their ranks and their individual [descriptions]...
The transmitted commentaries mostly follow the author’s own interpretations; as for the explicit texts of the sūtras and śāstras, they were not included.

Now, I have undertaken this editing to preserve the work from beginning to end. Thus, I have removed the superfluous and supplemented the omissions to assist the original intention.孤山 (Gushan) once said:
The ailments of later times are just like the ailments of former times; if there should be anything that remains unsettled, we shall wait for future sages.

It is our hope merely that the traces of the heavenly deities’ protection and the foundation of the Great Power’s responsive manifestations will not lose their correctness and shall instead return to this very principle.
At the end of the second month of autumn in the Gui-si year of the Qiandao era, at the Huayan Aranya west of Futian,
I recorded this to resolve the disputes concerning the general and specific stages of the sequence.
The text of the *Bai lu* (Record of the Hundred) states: "The Great Brahmā Deva, the Trāyastriṃśa Devas, the Four World-Protecting Kings, Vajrapāṇi, Guhyapada, the General Saṃjñeya,
the Great Eloquence Deva, the Merit Deva, Hārītī, and her five hundred retinues, including the Mother of Ghosts (*Pūtanā*)—

these are listed here according to the *Guishen pin* (Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits) of the *Guanzhi jing* (Sutra of Contemplation of the Wisdom-Knowledge), compiled and arranged from beginning to end."
As for this, Master Siming moved the positions of Guṇakārandavyūha and Mahāprajñā to the rear;
his separate invocation was based on the text within the *Vaiśravaṇa-parivarta*. Master Ciyun, however, moved only Guṇadevī to the rear;
his separate invocation was based on the *Guṇadevī-parivarta*. Having made offerings to the Buddha, he separately offered incense, flowers, and various kinds of fine delicacies.
[They] bestow [this] upon me. Because of this, ancient and modern [scholars] have each relied on their respective scriptural texts to mutually exclude one another.
Now, in order to settle these disputes, I shall examine them by means of the sūtras and śāstras. Generally, there are two ways of listing the celestial ranks.

One is the general arrangement as found in the assemblies of the Buddhas, where the Brahmā kings, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others are placed at the forefront, following the sequence in the *Baolu* (Record of the Hundred [Rituals]). This is because it does not pertain to a single session.
The arrangement of these [passages] is such that the texts before and after the "Light" section are not uniform, due to the distinction between general and specific [contexts].

Furthermore, in the *Mayūra-vidyārājñī-sūtra*, it mentions the Lord of the Sahā World, Brahmā Devarāja, Śakra Devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the twenty-eight great yakṣas, stating that the textual passages in other sūtras are not found in a single location.
This is like the court protocol of the world, where there are distinctions of honor, humility, rank, and status.

Each shall be settled in its proper place. Although there may occasionally be some lack of order, those of Brahmā and Śakra must necessarily come first, for they are the lords of the world and were the first to provide protection during the Buddha’s eight stages of manifestation.

Second, one should single-mindedly practice the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* according to the instructions of Goddess Puṇyavatī, in order to invoke the power of blessings to assist both the speaker and the listener.
One should specially install images of Puṇyavatī and Mahāprajñā to the left and right of the Buddha’s seat.

Next, the Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings are arranged separately at the head [of the assembly]. This is like the world’s practice of selecting excellent generals, who are specially distinguished and ranked above their peers.
Thus, the *Bai lu* (Record of the Hundred) instructs that images of Śrīdevī be placed to the left and right of the Buddha’s seat;
the intention is to honor this deity alone, providing her with a specially prepared fine seat in accordance with the scriptural text.

It is for this reason. Furthermore, the *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Matters) states: "If the dharma hall is spacious, one may additionally install seats for Mahāpratibhāna and the Four Heavenly Kings;
therefore, later generations further added Brahmā, Śakra, and others. From this, we know that the establishment of a single seat is not the standard ritual.
Moreover, as for those who have traditionally arranged images of the sixteen devas since ancient times, they all select the foremost among each group.

Regarding their respective presiding deities: furthermore, in terms of their manifest functions of admonishing and protecting through speech and conduct, although what they preside over differs for each, their actual purpose—generating goodness and extinguishing evil—is the same.
Moreover, if one considers their fundamental nature, there are none who are not great Bodhisattvas;
if one follows the sequential order, it is entirely from the perspective of their manifested traces. Furthermore, among the sixteen positions, [the deity] Maheśvara corresponds to...
There are two deities. The one currently being offered to is the Great Lord Maheśvara himself, the sovereign lord; he is not the same as the one among the yakṣas who bears that name.

Furthermore, regarding the goddess Hārītī, the Mother of Ghosts, she was originally but a single figure, though sometimes divided into two deities, as is clearly explained in detail in her own biography.
For now, I shall first set forth the sequence of those presiding over the regular Buddhist assemblies.
He is the Great Brahmā Deva King, the sovereign of the Sahā world, whose commands are uniquely honored;
he is the male ruler of the earth-dwelling worlds, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Honored Deva Śakra.
The World-Protecting Great Yakṣa King Vaiśravaṇa, Lord of the North;
his son, Virūḍhaka, Lord of the Kumbhāṇḍas, Protector of the East;
and his son, Virūpākṣa, the Great Nāga King, Protector of the West.
The one who has personally subdued the Maras and demons, vowing to act as the sovereign lord of the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada;
the Mahādeva Hārītīśvara who dwells at the summit of the realm of form;
the Great General Vaiśravaṇa, leader of the twenty-eight divisions and commander of all spirits and deities. Male.
The Great Goddess of Eloquence, who can bestow the great mass of wisdom and the dhāraṇīs;
the Great Goddess of Merit, who grants the fulfillment of all requests according to one's needs;
the Veda-deva, male and female, who with deep concern provide external protection for the fourfold assembly throughout the three continents.
The Earth Deity Sthāvarā, who increases, gives birth, and witnesses merit;
the Bodhi Tree Deity Vanavāsī, who provides shade over the site of enlightenment and whose cause and fruit mutually adorn one another;
the Ghost-Child Mother (Hārītī), who gives birth to various kings of ghosts and protects both male and female spirits.
Moving before the sun and moon to rescue those in the perils of war and weapons—this concludes the sixteen positions up to the deity Mārīcī.
Furthermore, there are those who add [deities] to make twenty positions.
One hundred are named "Beneficial Birth," and one thousand are "Radiant Light Dispelling Darkness. These are the Sons of Heaven of the Solar Palace.
The Lord of Stars and King of Constellations; the Prince of the Moon Palace who Coolly Illuminates the Night;
the Master of the Secret Treasury of the Dharma Jewel; the Sovereign Over All Dragons, the Sāgara-rāja;
the One Who Wields Authority over the Profound Darkness as the Lord of the Hell of Yama.

Furthermore, there are those who add deities such as those of the *fengshui* (geomancy) and supernatural powers to the preceding thirty-three positions, designating them as the "Thirty-three Heavens" (*Trāyastriṃśa*).
While it would do no harm to add more [deities], one should not specifically designate them as the Thirty-three Heavens.
Above this is the standard sequence for the arrangement of the Buddha’s assembly. However, within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), then...
To the left of the Buddha, place an image of Śrīdevī; to the right, place an image of Mahāprajñādevī.

As for Brahmā, Śakra, and the others, they should be arranged separately on both sides in their respective order. Those with discernment are requested to reflect upon this thoroughly; yet I fear even this may not yet be fully understood.
Now, I shall present this diagram so that the positions of the various ranks are clearly delineated, and thus, naturally, there will be no dispute.

As for the term "Mahābrahmā," it is called "Brahmā" because the wording is abbreviated. In the Western Regions, it is called *Bramana*; here it is translated as "Free from Desire" (*vītarāga*). Alternatively, it is said:

Pure, or as it is called, "extremely pure. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "With body and mind wondrously perfect and complete, their majestic deportment flawless, and endowed with pure prohibitive precepts as well as clear awakening—such a person, at that time, can lead the Brahma host as a Great Brahma King.
Above the Heaven of Self-Transformation and Others' Transformation are the Four Dhyānas, comprising eighteen heavens in total. Within the First Dhyāna, there are three heavens.

These are known as the Brahma-pāriṣadyas, the Brahma-purohitas, and the Mahābrahmās. Although there are fifteen heavens above them in the three dhyāna realms, within those realms there is no internal discursive thought and externally there is no speech;
they savor only the joy of meditative concentration (dhyāna-prīti). Since all are governed by the Brahma-heaven, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states:

"Next is the Brahma-heaven, which governs and encompasses the Brahma-folk and perfects the Brahma-conduct. The *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) states: "The Brahma King issues his commands."

Summarizing the above and concluding with the following: Jingxi stated that Brahmā is the lord of the *rūpadhātu* (the realm of form) and is also the lord of the three realms (*tridhātu*), while all others are his subjects.
This is because within this heaven there is *vitarka* and *vicāra* (applied and sustained thought), and externally there is speech.

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* refers to him as the Brahmā King who rules over a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūdika-lokadhātu*), as he dwells in the center of such a small chiliocosm. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to him as the Lord of the Sahā World, ruling over a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

He thus dwells in the midst of the great trichiliocosm and governs the remaining realms. It should be understood that horizontally he governs the small and great trichiliocosms, while vertically he encompasses all above and crowns all below;
he is collectively titled "King. His specific name is *Śikhin* in Sanskrit, which here means "Crest" (*dingji*).
It is also translated as "Spiral Crest" (*luoji*), because his fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) resembles a conch shell. The *Fahua wenju* states: "In foreign lands, fire is called..."
Śuddhodana. Because this king had previously cultivated the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), he destroyed the afflictions of the desire realm. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The Great Brahmā King has no separate location; it is simply the high pavilion within the Brahmakāyika Heaven that is called the Great Brahmā King.
His body is one and a half *yojanas* in height, his body is the color of white silver, and both his palace and his clothing are yellow."
His complexion is golden, and his lifespan is one and a half kalpas. The *Āgama Sūtras* state that when the various Brahmās descend, they all possess human forms.

The *Scriptures and Vinaya of Diverse Characteristics* states that the countenance of the Brahmā King is like that of a youth. The *Dharma Garden* states that the devas of the Form Realm do not wear clothing;

even if they were wearing it, it would appear no different. Although their heads lack topknots, they resemble celestial crowns. They have no male or female forms; their characteristics are solely [one].
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are correlated with the ten kings; thus, the Brahmā King is a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calculates the merit of Brahmā as follows: "The merit of all people filling the continent of Jambudvīpa does not equal the merit of one person in Aparagoyānī.
The merit of all people filling Aparagoyānī does not equal the merit of one person in Pūrvavideha. Filling [Pūrvavideha]...

The merit of all humans combined does not equal the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru; likewise, the merit of the assemblies of the heavens up to the sixth heaven does not equal the merit of a single person in the Brahma Heaven.

Furthermore, by cultivating the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one receives retribution as a celestial king. According to the *Qiufa zhuan* (Account of Seeking the Dharma): [text continues].
When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Brahmā stood at the Buddha’s right side, holding a white fly-whisk as he descended.
After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, Brahmā offered him his palace and requested that he turn the Wheel of Dharma. In the *Saptabuddhastotravidhi-sūtra*, Brahmā addressed the Buddha:

"If there is a king who wishes to protect his kingdom during times of calamity and pestilence, he should uphold this mantra of mine and contemplate it with single-minded meditative concentration. [This shall quell] all epidemics..."
The ghosts quickly departed from that country. There are numerous texts of this kind concerning the protection of the Dharma. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Aśvajit did not know where the four great elements would be extinguished without remainder;

he questioned the King of Brahmā, who then took Aśvajit by the hand and led him outside the assembly, saying, "Why do you not ask the Buddha? The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: The King of Brahmā spoke...
The sound was pure and wondrous. Each member of the Brahmā assembly thought to themselves that the Brahmā King was speaking to them alone; it reached equally far and near. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When the seer Vasiṣṭha debated with the Brahmā King, [the King] manifested three eyes upon his face for him to see.

A verse from the *Kalpa Chapter* says: "He dwelt alone for one period of increase and decrease; subsequently, mindful of the welfare of sentient beings, he brought forth their birth—this constitutes the formation eon (*vivartakalpa*)."
At the beginning, the Great Brahmā King was born after the Brahmā-purohitas and the Brahmakāyikas; therefore, he conceived the notion that "I am the one who can create.
In the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Brahmā King said: "I see the Buddha-field of Śākyamuni as being like the palace of Maheśvara."
Regarding the reason why the Buddha-land of Treasure Adornment (Ratnavyūha) is placed at the head of the present assembly of Buddhas, there are five reasons for this intention:

first, he is the sovereign who issues commands throughout the three realms; second, he is one who descended from the Buddha’s realm to be born here; third, he is the one who requested the turning of the wheel of Dharma;

fourth, he is ranked foremost among those who propagate and protect the various sutras; and fifth, according to the *Bai lu* (Records of the Hundred), his request is designated as being at the beginning.

It was formerly transmitted that the *Engi-kei* (Record of Origins) held the bell; however, as the *Rokujōroku-mon* (Inquiries from the Six-Volume Record) notes that "pierced eyes" (*gan-zaku-mu*) are neither prominent nor essential, it is not appended here.

Other texts follow this precedent. Nevertheless, the *Tangen-ki* (Record of Exploring the Profundities), citing the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, states that there are seven kinds of attaining Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
First, constructing a caitya where none existed before; second, establishing a saṃghārāma; third, reconciling a dispersed saṃgha;
fourth, cultivating the four immeasurables; fifth, serving as parents to the Buddha’s life; sixth, personally leaving the household life and teaching others to leave the household life;
seventh, erecting the banner of the Dharma. If a person performs even one of these seven deeds, they will attain rebirth in the Brahma Heaven. This is so.
It is known that one is born as a Brahmā in the first dhyāna heaven by virtue of these seven types of karma; how much more so for a king?
Therefore, those who delight in merit need not exert themselves excessively to cultivate it. Furthermore, regarding the measure of this "Brahma-merit" (*brahmapuṇya*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
the amount of karma required by sentient beings to produce a single trichiliocosm [world-system] constitutes the measure of one unit of Brahma-merit.
It is even more superior. When the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* compares the merit of the six heavens, the measure of the merit of even a single Brahmā-deva is already such;
how much more so for the Brahmā-rāja! This is why one should offer worship to honor the Buddhist assembly. The eulogy says:
When our Buddha descended from the heavens to be born among men, Mahābrahmā led the way before him, holding a white fly-whisk, or sometimes standing to his right.
He offered his celestial palace as a tribute; O Auspicious Master, we pray that you turn the Wheel of Dharma.
True Sovereign of the world, you who govern millions of billions of lands and subdue the borderlands.
Among the eighteen Brahmās, he obeys their commands; Thus, from the upper and lower realms, all rely upon him for refuge.
His body is six thousand li in height; his lifespan lasts one and a half kalpas.
His wondrous complexion is like white silver, and his head is crowned with a topknot. He is known by the specific name Śikhin, who destroyed heterodox thoughts.
The six heavens of the desire realm cannot rival his merit; With pure and bright precepts, he maintains majestic deportment.
He protects the Dharma, protects the nation, and protects those who practice the Way; He specially summons various scriptures and always holds them in high esteem.
Though he is reckoned as the father of sentient beings, His celestial palaces and Buddha-lands move in constant accord with him.
Desiring to be born therein, one cultivates the seven kinds of merit: Building Buddhist temples and establishing caityas, bringing sentient beings into harmony, and saving their fathers' lives;
Raising high the banner of Dharma to deliver all who have the capacity for awakening, leading both self and others into the homeless life beyond the sea of desire;
Joyfully relinquishing immeasurable wealth and extensively practicing great compassion.
Hearing that this holy power is inconceivable, one should first reverently honor and look up to his numinous countenance.
"Śakra Devendra" is transmitted as "Diśì" (帝釋).
This is a case where both the Indic and Chinese names are cited, though the phrasing is abbreviated. In Sanskrit, it is called Śakrendra, or simply Śakra.
Śakra-devānām-indra—this is translated as "The Capable Heavenly Lord" (Neng Tian Di) or "The Capable Lord of Devas" (Neng Tian Zhu).

In the *Abhidharmakośa*, the full Sanskrit term is given as Śakra-devānām-indra. Here, taking the character "Śak" from the Sanskrit and the character "Di" (Lord) from the Chinese, they are combined to form "Dishi" (Emperor-Release).
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other texts, the Buddha refers to him by the name Kauśika. [This was his original...]
It has one thousand names, which have not been fully translated; they shall be indicated individually according to the text.

As for its location, it is situated on the summit of Mount Sumeru, the second heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). In Sanskrit it is called *Trāyastriṃśa*, which translates here as "Thirty-three.
This is because, during their causal stage, thirty-three people once practiced sublime deeds together with him in the kingdom of Magadha—constructing bridges, digging wells, and creating gardens.
Śakra was born together with Lady Śakuntalā through their shared karma and common practice. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"In the past, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa, there was a woman who resolved to build a stūpa, and thirty-two people assisted her. They have now been reborn together in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
for this reason, there are thirty-two celestial palaces surrounding the heavens, in the midst of which Śakra resides."
Therefore, it is said there are thirty-three [gods]. Because Śakra was the leader during his causal stage, he was reborn as the Heavenly King.
He has three consorts: Ālambusā, Sūtrāmanī, and Cūṭamālā. To the northeast of his palace is the Ālambusā grove; to the southwest is the Sudharmā Hall.
Whenever Śakra ascends to that hall, he assembles the celestial hosts to preach the Dharma. If Śakra is not present there...

In this hall, whenever the various devas arrive, they invariably pay reverence to its seat. Its physical dimensions are one *li*, and it is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, which the other devas do not possess.
As for the limit of its lifespan, one hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night there.
Thirty days constitute a month; twelve months constitute a year. Thirty-six thousand human years constitute one [celestial] year.
Thus, when their lifespan reaches ten such years, they hold a vajra-precious mallet in their hands, signifying supreme nobility and the repelling of enemies.
Therefore, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states that Śakra possesses this, and it is difficult for those of meager merit to behold. Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa-sūtra speaks of "Śakra’s vajra."
The Precious Vajra can destroy the asuras. The *Jingtu sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Pure Land) states:

"The thirty-two ministers who serve Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and the four Great Kings of the Quarters—the Lords of Fate and the Registrars—descend to this realm on various days of ritual observance to examine the deeds of men regarding their blessings and calamities."

Except for those certain to die and be reborn, they are recorded in the texts and scriptures. If this is so, then horizontally he presides over the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and vertically there is nothing from the Cāturmahārājika Heaven downward that he does not govern. The *Wenju* (Textual Explanations) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"Śakra, together with eighty billion nayutas of celestial maidens, indulges in unrestrained play; looking east, he forgets the west, yet his desire remains unsated. He then transforms into—

The aged asura Nahuṣa caused the devas to forget their bodies and lose their heads. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that there is a great elephant capable of transforming its body to entertain with the devas.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that a bodhisattva on the third bhūmi often acts as the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Tiantai says that in the Āgamas, Śakra is an anāgāmin; however, in the Separate and Complete Teachings, Śakra is...
He will dwell in the *Lengyan Samādhi* (*Śūraṅgama-samādhi*) during his tenure as a Śākya, and in the future he shall attain Buddhahood, named *Amogha* (The Unattached).

According to the *Xiyu Ji*, when the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, [he] constructed a flight of stairs of the seven precious gems; standing to the Buddha’s left, he held a parasol of the seven precious gems while attending the Buddha on the descent.
Together with the Brahmā King, he requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma. The Buddha subsequently preached numerous sūtras within his palace. [He stood] by the Buddha’s...
During his causal stage, he repeatedly manifested as a human being; at times, he transformed himself into lions, hawks, or pigeons to test the resolve of others.

He fought against the asuras, fled from charging chariots, and encountered a golden soaring bird nesting in a tree. Seeing eggs about to hatch, he ordered his charioteer to turn the vehicle back, refusing to harm them.
His acts of inducing others to practice giving and his various manifestations were not limited to these instances alone. The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) states:
When Śakra, for the sake of Mahākāśyapa, went from house to house begging as a poor man, he manifested himself as a poor husband and wife weaving mats for their livelihood.
They offered food to Kāśyapa and sought his blessings without satiety. When the five signs of decline appeared, they fell into the womb of a donkey.

Hearing the Three Refuges from a human being, their virtuous minds were reborn; they returned to being Śakras and received celestial blessings. (From a separate translation of the *Aṣṭama-bhikṣu-sūtra*).

The *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) records: There was a yakṣa whose form was extremely small and whose complexion was black and hideous; he sat upon the throne of the Heavenly Emperor.
All thirty-three gods were filled with great wrath and indignation. Śakra, the Heavenly Emperor, said, "This one is named the 'Anger-Assisting Ghost' (*Krodhānukārin*).
He then bared his right shoulder, held a censer in his hand, and addressed the yakṣa, saying three times, 'Great Seer, I am Śakra, the Heavenly Emperor.'"

The yakṣa’s form grew smaller and smaller until it vanished. Thus we know that although he occupied the exalted rank of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, his compassion did not harm living beings and his pursuit of merit never faltered.
